summary: Describes MISTY1, a secret-key block cipher with a 128-bit key, a 64-bit block, and a variable number of rounds. It documents the algorithm, including key scheduling.

plainLanguage.summary: MISTY1 is a recipe for scrambling data with a secret key, written down so others can use it.

subtitle: A block cipher algorithm with provable security against cryptanalysis.

tldr.problem: Block cipher algorithms need to balance security (resistance to cryptanalysis) with performance (speed on both hardware and software). Designing ciphers with provable security properties is difficult.
tldr.mechanism: MISTY1 is a 128-bit key, 64-bit block cipher with a variable number of rounds. It uses a key scheduling phase to expand the key, and a data randomizing phase with functions FO, FI, and FL that apply substitution and permutation operations. The design is based on the theory of provable security against differential and linear cryptanalysis.
tldr.outcome: MISTY1 achieves strong security properties (differential and linear characteristic probabilities of 2^-140 with 8 rounds) while maintaining practical performance (40–57 Mbps on CPUs, 512 Mbps on hardware).

today: RFC 2994 is an Informational document describing the MISTY1 algorithm. It has not been obsoleted. MISTY1 remains available for both academic and commercial use under the licensing terms described.

sections.title: MISTY1 Overview
sections.content:
MISTY1 is a block cipher—a recipe for scrambling fixed-size chunks of data. It takes a 128-bit secret key and scrambles a 64-bit block of data. The number of encryption rounds is variable, but 8 rounds is recommended for most uses. The algorithm was designed by Mitsubishi Electric to achieve both strong security and high speed.

Block ciphers are foundational cryptographic primitives used in many protocols. MISTY1 is relevant because it demonstrates how to design a cipher with provable security—formal proof that it resists known attacks. The implementation evidence shows MISTY1 can encrypt data at 40–57 Mbps on CPUs and 512 Mbps on hardware, making it practical for real systems.
sections.plainLanguage: MISTY1 is a way to scramble data. You give it a secret key and some data, and it produces scrambled data. With the key, you can unscramble it. The secret is in the recipe.

sections.title: Key Scheduling: Expanding the Key
sections.content:
The algorithm has two main parts. The first is key scheduling. MISTY1 takes a 128-bit input key and expands it into a larger set of subkeys, stored as expanded key (EK) entries. Each EK entry is 16 bits. The key expansion uses a function called FI, which itself uses substitution tables (S-boxes).

The key scheduling phase produces 32 subkeys from the original 128-bit key. These subkeys are derived by applying the FI function in a specific pattern so that changing even one bit of the input key causes many bits of the output subkeys to change. This property, called the avalanche effect, strengthens the cipher against key-recovery attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of the key as a seed. The key scheduling plants it and grows a big tree of random-looking numbers (subkeys) from it. Each subkey is used in a different part of the scrambling recipe.

sections.title: Data Randomizing: The Encryption Process
sections.content:
The second part is data randomizing. MISTY1 splits the 64-bit plaintext into two 32-bit halves and applies a series of rounds. Each round uses three functions: FO, FI, and FL. FO and FI apply complex substitutions and permutations. FL is a function that mixes the data using subkey bits. The rounds alternate between the two halves and each other.

With 8 rounds, the structure is: rounds 0 through 7 (with FL applied in even-numbered rounds), followed by a final application of FL. Decryption reverses this process in the opposite order using an inverse function FLINV instead of FL. The substitution tables S7 (128 entries of 7 bits each) and S9 (512 entries of 9 bits each) are fixed and public, only the subkeys are secret.
sections.plainLanguage: Scrambling happens in rounds, like a shuffle. Each round takes the data, applies the subkeys in a tricky way with lookup tables, and mixes it up. After 8 rounds, the data is thoroughly scrambled.

sections.title: Security and Provable Resistance
sections.content:
MISTY1 was designed with proven security against two major attack classes: differential cryptanalysis and linear cryptanalysis. With 8 rounds, the probability of a differential characteristic is 2^-140 and the probability of a linear characteristic is also 2^-140. For comparison, DES has differential characteristic probability of 2^-62 and linear characteristic probability of 2^-46. This means MISTY1 is dramatically more resistant.

The design was based on theoretical work by Nyberg, Knudsen, and Matsui on building ciphers with provable security bounds. These proofs do not mean the cipher cannot be broken—they mean that an attacker using differential or linear techniques will need an unrealistic amount of computation and data.
sections.plainLanguage: Mathematicians proved that to break MISTY1 by trying known tricks would take so much work that it is not practical. That is what 'provable security' means.

sections.title: Usage, Performance, and Licensing
sections.content:
MISTY1 can be used in different modes. The document defines MISTY1-CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode with a standard object identifier for use in protocols and cryptographic systems. Implementations on Pentium II/266MHz achieved 57 Mbps in CBC mode, and on PA-7200/120MHz achieved 40 Mbps. A prototype hardware implementation reached 512 Mbps.

Regarding licensing, MISTY1 is freely available for academic (non-profit) use. For commercial use, Mitsubishi Electric offers a licensing agreement. This tiered licensing model made MISTY1 a viable option for both research and industry deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: MISTY1 runs fast on computers and even faster on special chips. You can use it for free if you are doing research, or license it from Mitsubishi if you are selling products.
